When I go RVing, I tow a small car behind it. Often, you can find a parking lot that'll let you hang out and just use that as your base. Then, when you do that, you really only need a campground for the facilities. The 'dual sport bike' is a good idea, and I have met some folks who brought a pair of them with them.

But, having made many sojourns similar to this, I'd REALLY suggest you do two things. First, double check everything you "know" to be true (such as camping on bases). Second, do NOT sell your house right away - make a trial run, even if it means you experience living out of your car for a month or two.

As you were in the military, I'm quite certain they taught you how to pack. You can fit quite a bit of stuff into a car. Try that and see if you like it, and do so before selling your house. You may find that you really, really don't like it. It's amazing how isolated it can be, even if you're traveling to populated areas.

There's lots of things you can do to make it interesting. For example, even with plenty of money, I registered to work with one of the day labor places and I'd go into a different area, hook up with them, and do a few days of manual labor. By not needing the money, it meant I could be pretty selective about the jobs that I took. They share files across the country, so you only really need to register with them once. (I used Labor Ready.)

This let me meet new and interesting people, and have something of a social life. As they're people that are actually wanting to work, it meant they were generally good people.

The road gets lonely and finding a way to keep it interesting might help you. Also, CB radios are still in use and you might be surprised about how many areas aren't covered by cellular service.

I've done a trip cross country twice, over a week sleeping in a 2011 mazda3, solo. Driving through the southern states was some of the most beautiful sights I've seen, and miss that.

Met a 6'4 Cherokee girl on craigslist rideshare, one of the coolest people I've ever. She paid me 300 bucks to pick her up in Denver and drop her off in Sacramento. She and I took turns driving, would stop a few times just to take pictures of mountains in Utah, for example. I know I'll enjoy it.

I will look into the labor ready, that's sounds like something I can use to meet cool people, thanks a bunch.

Also, stay safe. An RV actually counts as your residence, in most jurisdictions. So, treat it like that and keep a firearm handy for protection. Things can go pear-shaped quickly.

Eventually, you'll either get tired of the open road or your RV will be too expensive to maintain and repair. You can prolong that by being pretty picky about maintaining it. Yeah, oil changes are more expensive (and you'll have to use truck stop types of places to have the facility large enough to fit your RV), and they'll charge you more to rotate your tires - but it's in your best interest to do so.

If you can't tell, I've done similar - quite a bit. If you REALLY want to get adventurous, you can find cheap shipping (it won't be quick) and ship your RV to a different continent. I cheated and just rented an RV and tooled around Europe for a couple of months.

It's a great adventure, and you'll learn many things. I highly recommend other folks consider taking the time to make these types of treks. You only live once, and you might as well get to experience it in the fullest. But, it really makes a big difference if you've planned everything well enough. It helps to know what to expect and to have alternate options.

And, again, crossing the country is a whole lot different than living on the road for months at a time. I really suggest trying it in a car for at least a couple of months. If you do, you may find that you just want to tour part time - and not sell your house. Having a house to go back to seems like an idea worth considering.

If you're mechanically savvy, you can get a used RV and then go over it with a fine tooth comb. The depreciation on an RV is insane, so they're not very expensive. Chances are, you can find one with fairly low miles and fairly good condition.

Why yes, yes I am urging you to be cautious when it comes to selling your house.

In my experience, and this is just mine, it gets old after about six months. I did eight months and a full year, but the full year was when I also did some of my traveling outside of the US. There are only so many ways to make every day interesting and there are only so many roadside attractions. It looks a lot more interesting than it really is.

That said, you could possibly document your travels - maybe even making a blog and sharing videos/pictures. If you're interested in that aspect, I'm pretty sure I can get you squared away.

I planned on starting a youtube channel and maybe an Instagram or some other social media to document everything. And selling my house isn't just to RV full time, I have full intentions of going back home in California. My parents own a large plot in Northern CA, with RV hookups.

That makes good sense. A fallback plan is important and kinda what I was getting at. Having an 'out' is a good thing and will maybe help release some stress should you discover it's not something you want to do for long. It's comforting to say, "Yup... I can stop this crazy shit any time I want."

I try not to say it, but it gets old fast when you're on the road - doubly so if you're doing it alone and you didn't mention a spouse or significant other. I try to avoid coming right out and saying that it really can start to suck, because I'm of the opinion that more folks should try it. 'Snot easy, but an RV makes it so much easier.
